artifacts.name: Change Request Form
artifacts.description: A formal document requesting a change to the agreed project scope, timeline, budget, or approach, including the rationale, impact assessment, and options for the change authority to consider.
artifacts.purpose: Change requests ensure that modifications to the project baseline are considered formally, with full understanding of their impact on scope, time, cost, and quality. They prevent uncontrolled scope creep and maintain governance oversight.
artifacts.whenToUse: Submit whenever a change to the agreed baseline is needed — new requirements, scope changes, timeline adjustments, or budget increases. The change authority (usually the project board) decides whether to approve.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Describe the requested change clearly — what specifically needs to change and why? Reference the current baseline that would be affected.

Explain the rationale — what has changed since the baseline was agreed? Is this driven by new requirements, external factors, or issues discovered during delivery?

Assess the impact on all project dimensions: scope, timeline, cost, quality, and risk. Be honest about trade-offs.

Present options where possible: the full change, a reduced version, or alternative approaches that achieve the same outcome with less impact.

Include a recommendation and the consequences of not making the change.
tips: Be specific about what changes and what stays the same.
Quantify the impact — how many days/weeks delay, how much additional cost.
Present options, not just the change — give the decision-maker choices.
Include the consequence of not approving the change.
Keep the form concise — decision-makers need clarity, not volume.
commonMistakes: Submitting vague change requests without clear impact assessment.
Not presenting alternatives or options for the change authority.
Bundling multiple changes into one request, making it hard to approve partially.
Not explaining the consequence of rejection.
Submitting changes after they have already been implemented.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, significant changes may require updated spend control approval from CDDO. Changes affecting service scope may trigger a need for re-assessment against the GDS Service Standard. Budget changes above delegated limits require ministerial or finance director approval. artifacts.name: Status Report / Highlight Report
artifacts.description: A periodic report summarising project progress, achievements, upcoming activities, risks, issues, and decisions needed, providing governance bodies with the information they need to oversee the project effectively.
artifacts.purpose: Status reports keep governance bodies informed and enable timely intervention when projects deviate from plan. They provide a regular checkpoint for progress, surface issues requiring escalation, and maintain stakeholder confidence through transparency.
artifacts.whenToUse: Produce at regular intervals — typically weekly for delivery teams and monthly for project boards. The frequency should match the governance cadence and the pace of change on the project.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the overall RAG (Red/Amber/Green) status for the project and for each dimension: scope, time, cost, and quality. Be honest — amber and red statuses are not failures, they are signals that attention is needed.

Summarise key achievements since the last report — what has been delivered, decided, or unblocked?

Outline planned activities for the next period — what will the team focus on?

Highlight risks and issues that need governance attention — especially those requiring decisions or escalation.

Include any decisions needed from the board and any changes to the project baseline.
tips: Be honest with RAG statuses — hiding problems erodes trust and delays intervention.
Keep it concise — one to two pages maximum. Boards do not have time for lengthy reports.
Focus on exceptions — what has changed since last time, not a repeat of the plan.
Include specific asks — what decisions or actions do you need from the board?
Use consistent format so readers know where to find information quickly.
commonMistakes: Always reporting green when problems exist — this destroys credibility.
Making reports too long — busy executives will not read multi-page reports.
Not including specific asks or decisions needed from the governance body.
Reporting activities rather than outcomes — what was achieved, not just what was done.
Not explaining RAG status changes — why has something moved from green to amber?

artifacts.name: Terms of Reference (ToR)
artifacts.description: A document defining the purpose, scope, membership, authority, and operating procedures of a governance body such as a board, committee, or working group.
artifacts.purpose: Terms of Reference establish clear expectations for governance bodies, ensuring members understand their role, authority, and responsibilities. They prevent scope creep in governance, clarify decision-making authority, and ensure meetings are productive.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create when establishing any new governance body — project boards, architecture review boards, steering committees, or working groups. Review annually or when the body's remit changes.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the purpose of the governance body — why does it exist and what value does it add? Be specific about what it governs and what is outside its remit.

List the membership: chair, standing members, and invited attendees. Define quorum requirements and deputy arrangements.

Specify the authority: what decisions can this body make? What requires escalation? What is delegated to sub-groups or individuals?

Define operating procedures: meeting frequency, agenda management, paper submission deadlines, minute-taking, and action tracking.

Include the relationship to other governance bodies — what feeds into this body and what does it feed into?
tips: Be explicit about decision-making authority — can the body decide, or only recommend?
Define quorum clearly — decisions made without quorum may be challenged.
Include paper submission deadlines so members have time to prepare.
Review ToR annually to ensure they remain fit for purpose.
Keep membership small enough for effective decision-making (5-9 members ideal).
commonMistakes: Not defining decision-making authority clearly, leading to confusion about what the body can actually decide.
Making membership too large, preventing effective discussion and decision-making.
Not specifying quorum, allowing decisions to be made without adequate representation.
Writing ToR and never reviewing them as the governance landscape changes.
Not clarifying the relationship with other governance bodies, creating overlaps or gaps.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, Terms of Reference should align with the Government Functional Standard for Project Delivery (GovS 002) and departmental governance frameworks. They should clarify the relationship between project governance and departmental governance structures. artifacts.name: Governance Framework Document
artifacts.description: A comprehensive document defining the governance structure for a programme or organisation, including all governance bodies, their relationships, decision-making authority, escalation paths, and operating principles.
artifacts.purpose: The governance framework ensures that decisions are made at the right level by the right people with the right information. It provides clarity on authority, prevents bottlenecks, and ensures appropriate oversight without creating bureaucracy.
artifacts.whenToUse: Define at programme initiation and review at major phase boundaries. Essential for programmes with multiple projects, multiple teams, or cross-organisational delivery.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Map the governance landscape: what bodies exist, what is their purpose, and how do they relate to each other? Show the hierarchy from strategic (portfolio board) through programme to project level.

For each governance body, define its purpose, authority, membership, and cadence. Use Terms of Reference for detailed specification.

Define decision-making authority at each level: what can be decided at project level, what needs programme approval, and what requires portfolio or ministerial sign-off?

Establish escalation paths: how do issues, risks, and decisions flow upward when they cannot be resolved at a lower level?

Define the governance principles: proportionality, transparency, accountability, and efficiency. Governance should enable delivery, not obstruct it.
tips: Design governance to be proportionate to risk — lightweight for low-risk decisions, rigorous for high-risk.
Define clear escalation triggers so teams know when to escalate without being told.
Include delegated authority limits — financial, contractual, and technical.
Review governance effectiveness periodically — is it enabling or blocking delivery?
Keep governance lean — every meeting and approval step has a cost.
commonMistakes: Creating too many governance bodies with overlapping remits.
Not defining delegated authority, forcing everything to senior level for decision.
Making governance too heavy, slowing delivery without adding proportionate value.
Not defining escalation triggers, leaving teams uncertain about when to escalate.
Designing governance on paper but not enforcing it in practice.

artifacts.name: Assurance Plan
artifacts.description: A plan defining how the project or programme will be assured — what reviews, assessments, and checks will be conducted, when, by whom, and against what criteria.
artifacts.purpose: The assurance plan ensures that independent scrutiny is applied at appropriate points to verify that the project is on track, following good practice, and likely to deliver its intended outcomes. It builds confidence for governance bodies and sponsors.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during project initiation as part of the Integrated Assurance and Approvals Plan (IAAP). Update as the project progresses and assurance needs become clearer.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Identify all assurance activities required: GDS service assessments, IPA gateway reviews, internal audits, security assessments, accessibility audits, and peer reviews.

For each assurance activity, define: what it assesses, when it occurs, who conducts it, what evidence is needed, and what the possible outcomes are.

Map assurance activities to the project timeline, ensuring they occur at appropriate decision points (before major investment decisions, phase transitions, or go-live).

Define how assurance findings will be addressed: who owns the response, what is the escalation path for critical findings, and how will progress be tracked?

Include self-assurance activities (internal reviews, quality checks) alongside independent assurance.
tips: Align assurance activities with decision points — assurance should inform decisions.
Book external assurance (GDS assessments, IPA reviews) well in advance — they have lead times.
Prepare evidence packs progressively, not in a last-minute rush before the review.
Treat assurance as helpful, not adversarial — assessors want you to succeed.
Track and close assurance recommendations promptly.
commonMistakes: Treating assurance as a compliance tick-box rather than a genuine quality check.
Not booking external reviews early enough, causing timeline delays.
Preparing for assessments at the last minute rather than building evidence continuously.
Not tracking or closing recommendations from previous assurance activities.
Only planning for external assurance and neglecting internal quality checks.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the Integrated Assurance and Approvals Plan (IAAP) is the standard approach. It should include GDS service assessments (at alpha, beta, and live), IPA gateway reviews (for major projects), CDDO spend control reviews, and departmental assurance activities. artifacts.name: Gate Review Checklist
artifacts.description: A structured checklist of criteria that must be satisfied before a project can proceed through a governance gate — typically at phase boundaries such as discovery-to-alpha, alpha-to-beta, or beta-to-live.
artifacts.purpose: Gate review checklists ensure that projects meet minimum quality and readiness criteria before progressing to the next phase. They prevent premature progression that leads to costly rework and provide a consistent standard across projects.
artifacts.whenToUse: Use at each phase boundary to assess readiness to proceed. Complete the checklist collaboratively with the project team and present to the governance body that approves phase transitions.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the criteria for each gate based on what should be true before the next phase begins. Group criteria by theme: user needs, technical readiness, team capability, governance, and commercial.

For each criterion, define what 'met' looks like — what evidence demonstrates that the criterion is satisfied?

Create a simple assessment scale: Met, Partially Met, Not Met. For partially met criteria, define what remediation is needed and whether it blocks progression.

Include both mandatory criteria (must be met to proceed) and advisory criteria (should be met but can proceed with a plan to address).

Document the decision: proceed, proceed with conditions, or do not proceed. Record any conditions and their owners.
tips: Align criteria with the GDS Service Standard for digital services.
Distinguish between blocking criteria and advisory criteria.
Complete the checklist collaboratively — it should not be a surprise to the team.
Use the checklist as a preparation tool, not just an assessment tool — share it early so teams can prepare.
Document the gate decision and any conditions clearly.
commonMistakes: Making the checklist so long that it becomes a bureaucratic burden rather than a quality check.
Not distinguishing between mandatory and advisory criteria.
Applying the same checklist regardless of project size and risk.
Using the checklist as a gotcha rather than a collaborative readiness assessment.
Not documenting conditions attached to a proceed decision.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, gate reviews should align with the GDS Service Standard (14 points) for digital services and the IPA gateway process for major projects. The GDS publishes specific criteria for alpha, beta, and live assessments. Departments may add additional criteria for security accreditation, data protection, and accessibility compliance. artifacts.name: Architecture Governance Board Paper
artifacts.description: A formal submission to an Architecture Review Board (ARB) or Architecture Governance Board presenting an architectural proposal, decision, or exception request for review and approval.
artifacts.purpose: ARB papers ensure that significant architectural decisions receive appropriate scrutiny from senior technical stakeholders. They maintain architectural consistency across programmes, ensure standards compliance, and manage technical risk at an enterprise level.
artifacts.whenToUse: Submit when making significant architectural decisions that affect multiple services, introduce new technology, deviate from standards, or have significant cost or risk implications. The ARB Terms of Reference should define what requires submission.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with a clear statement of what you are asking the ARB to do: approve a decision, endorse an approach, grant an exception, or provide guidance.

Provide context: what project or programme is this for, what problem are you solving, and what constraints apply?

Present the proposal or decision with sufficient technical detail for the board to assess it. Include architecture diagrams, technology choices, and integration impacts.

Show alignment with architecture principles, standards, and the target state architecture. If requesting an exception, explain why the standard cannot be met and what compensating controls are in place.

Include a risk assessment and the impact on other systems or teams.
tips: Be clear about what decision you need from the ARB — approve, advise, or note.
Provide enough detail for informed decision-making but do not overwhelm with unnecessary depth.
Show how the proposal aligns with (or deviates from) architecture principles and standards.
Include the impact on other teams and systems — the ARB thinks enterprise-wide.
Circulate the paper in advance so board members can prepare questions.
commonMistakes: Not being clear about what decision is needed from the board.
Presenting a fait accompli rather than a genuine proposal for review.
Not showing alignment with architecture principles and standards.
Omitting the impact on other systems and teams.
Submitting papers too late for board members to review properly.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, ARB papers should demonstrate alignment with the Technology Code of Practice, cross-government architecture principles, and departmental standards. They should reference relevant cross-government platforms and explain why they are or are not being used. artifacts.name: Spend Control Submission
artifacts.description: A formal submission to CDDO (Central Digital and Data Office) seeking approval for digital, data, and technology spend above departmental delegated authority thresholds.
artifacts.purpose: Spend control ensures that government technology spending delivers value for money, aligns with government strategy, and avoids duplication. It provides central oversight of significant technology investments and promotes use of shared platforms and open standards.
artifacts.whenToUse: Submit when planning technology spend above your department's delegated authority threshold (typically £100k-£1M depending on the department). Required before contracts are signed or significant expenditure begins.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the business need — what problem are you solving and for whom? Reference user research and policy objectives that drive the need.

Demonstrate alignment with the Technology Code of Practice — address each relevant point and explain how your approach complies.

Show that you have considered shared platforms and cross-government solutions before building bespoke. Explain why shared solutions are or are not appropriate.

Provide cost information: total cost of ownership over the contract/project lifetime, broken down by capital and revenue. Compare with alternatives.

Include the procurement approach, timeline, and any dependencies on other approvals.
tips: Engage with CDDO early — informal conversations before formal submission save time.
Demonstrate genuine consideration of shared platforms, not just a tick-box dismissal.
Be clear about what you are asking approval for — scope, cost, and timeline.
Address the Technology Code of Practice points explicitly.
Include evidence of user research and how it drives the technical approach.
commonMistakes: Submitting too late, creating timeline pressure that limits CDDO's ability to review properly.
Not demonstrating genuine consideration of cross-government shared platforms.
Providing insufficient cost information or unrealistic estimates.
Not addressing Technology Code of Practice compliance explicitly.
Treating spend control as a blocker rather than a quality assurance process.
artifacts.governmentContext: CDDO spend controls apply to all central government departments for digital, data, and technology spend above delegated thresholds. The process assesses alignment with the Technology Code of Practice, value for money, and strategic fit. CDDO may approve, approve with conditions, or reject submissions. artifacts.name: Service Assessment Evidence Pack
artifacts.description: A collection of evidence demonstrating how a digital service meets the 14 points of the GDS Service Standard, prepared for presentation at a service assessment (alpha, beta, or live).
artifacts.purpose: The evidence pack demonstrates to GDS assessors that the service team has met the Service Standard requirements. It provides structured evidence of user research, technical approach, team capability, and operational readiness appropriate to the assessment phase.
artifacts.whenToUse: Prepare in the weeks leading up to a GDS service assessment. Start collecting evidence from the beginning of each phase — do not leave it to the last minute. Update for each assessment phase (alpha, beta, live).
artifacts.howToBuild:
Structure the pack around the 14 points of the Service Standard. For each point, provide evidence appropriate to the assessment phase (expectations increase from alpha to beta to live).

For each point, include: a brief narrative explaining your approach, supporting evidence (screenshots, diagrams, research findings, metrics), and any known gaps with plans to address them.

Include a service overview: what the service does, who uses it, the team composition, and the technology stack.

Prepare a demo of the service — assessors will want to see it working. Ensure the demo environment is stable and representative.

Brief the team on the assessment format — it is a conversation, not a presentation. Team members should be prepared to answer questions about their area of expertise.
tips: Start collecting evidence from day one of each phase — do not leave it to the last minute.
The assessment is a conversation, not a presentation — prepare the team to discuss their work naturally.
Be honest about gaps and challenges — assessors respect transparency and want to help.
Show your working — assessors want to see the journey, not just the destination.
Practice with a mock assessment using colleagues from other teams.
commonMistakes: Leaving evidence collection to the last week before assessment.
Treating the assessment as a pass/fail exam rather than a peer review conversation.
Not preparing the whole team — assessors will ask different team members about their areas.
Hiding problems or gaps — assessors will find them and dishonesty damages credibility.
Over-preparing slides and presentations when assessors want conversation and demos.

The assessment panel typically includes a user researcher, designer, technical assessor, and product/delivery assessor. Outcomes are: met, not met, or met with conditions. Assessment reports are published on the GDS blog. Services that do not meet the standard cannot progress to the next phase without remediation.

artifacts.name: User Stories / Epics
artifacts.description: Short, simple descriptions of functionality from the perspective of the user, following the format 'As a [type of user], I want [goal] so that [benefit]'. Epics are large user stories that are broken down into smaller stories for delivery.
artifacts.purpose: User stories keep the team focused on delivering value to users rather than implementing technical specifications. They facilitate conversation between product owners and developers, and provide a unit of work that can be estimated, prioritised, and delivered within a sprint.
artifacts.whenToUse: Write user stories throughout discovery, alpha, and beta as user needs are identified and refined. Break epics into stories when they enter the sprint backlog. Stories should be small enough to complete within a single sprint.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with user research findings — what do users need to do? Express each need as a user story using the standard format: As a [user type], I want [goal], so that [benefit].

Add acceptance criteria — specific, testable conditions that must be true for the story to be considered complete. Use Given/When/Then format for clarity.

Estimate the story using story points or t-shirt sizes. If a story is too large to estimate confidently, it is probably an epic that needs breaking down.

Prioritise stories based on user value, dependencies, and risk. The product owner owns prioritisation with input from the team on technical dependencies.

Refine stories in backlog refinement sessions — add detail, clarify acceptance criteria, and identify dependencies before they enter a sprint.
tips: Keep stories small — if it cannot be completed in a sprint, break it down further.
Write acceptance criteria that are testable — they become your definition of done for that story.
Include non-functional acceptance criteria where relevant (performance, accessibility).
Use the INVEST criteria: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.
Link stories to user research evidence to maintain the connection to real user needs.
commonMistakes: Writing stories that are technical tasks rather than user-facing value.
Making stories too large to complete in a single sprint.
Not including acceptance criteria, leaving done undefined.
Writing stories without reference to actual user research.
Not refining stories before they enter a sprint, causing mid-sprint confusion.

artifacts.name: Definition of Done
artifacts.description: A shared checklist of criteria that must be satisfied before any piece of work (user story, feature, or increment) can be considered complete, ensuring consistent quality standards across the team.
artifacts.purpose: The Definition of Done creates a shared understanding of quality expectations, preventing incomplete work from being marked as done. It ensures that every increment is potentially releasable and reduces the accumulation of hidden technical debt.
artifacts.whenToUse: Define at the start of the project and refine as the team matures. Apply to every user story and sprint increment. Review and update at retrospectives when quality issues arise.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Collaborate with the whole team to define what done means. Include criteria across multiple dimensions: functionality, testing, documentation, deployment, and operational readiness.

Start with non-negotiable criteria: code reviewed, unit tests passing, acceptance criteria met, no critical bugs. Then add quality criteria: accessibility tested, performance acceptable, security scan clean.

Make criteria specific and verifiable — avoid vague statements like 'code is good quality'. Instead: 'code passes ESLint with zero warnings' or 'all new code has >80% test coverage'.

Display the Definition of Done prominently — on the team wall or in the project wiki. Reference it during sprint reviews when accepting work.

Evolve the DoD over time — as the team matures, add more criteria. If criteria are consistently met without effort, they may be too easy.
tips: Make it visible — print it and put it on the wall or pin it in the team channel.
Every team member should be able to recite the key criteria from memory.
Review it at retrospectives — if quality issues arise, the DoD may need strengthening.
Distinguish between story-level DoD and sprint-level DoD if needed.
Include accessibility and security criteria from the start, not as afterthoughts.
commonMistakes: Making the DoD so long that it becomes impractical to verify for every story.
Not enforcing the DoD consistently — exceptions erode the standard.
Not including non-functional criteria (accessibility, performance, security).
Defining DoD without team input, leading to lack of ownership.
Never updating the DoD as the team and project mature.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the Definition of Done should include accessibility testing (WCAG 2.2 AA), security scanning, and compliance with GDS design patterns. artifacts.name: Sprint/Iteration Plan
artifacts.description: A plan for a single sprint or iteration, defining the sprint goal, the user stories committed to, capacity allocation, and any known risks or dependencies for the sprint period.
artifacts.purpose: The sprint plan provides focus and commitment for the team during the sprint. It translates backlog priorities into a concrete plan of work, ensures the team is not over-committed, and provides a basis for daily progress tracking.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create at the start of each sprint during sprint planning. Reference throughout the sprint at daily standups. Review at sprint review and retrospective.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the sprint goal — a single sentence describing what the team aims to achieve this sprint. The goal should be meaningful to stakeholders, not just a list of stories.

Select stories from the top of the prioritised backlog that the team believes it can complete within the sprint, considering capacity (holidays, meetings, support duties).

Break stories into tasks and estimate effort. Ensure the total does not exceed team capacity. Leave buffer for unexpected work and support.

Identify dependencies and risks for the sprint — what could prevent completion? What needs to be resolved early?

Agree the plan as a team — commitment should be collective, not imposed.
tips: Define a clear sprint goal that gives meaning beyond just completing a list of stories.
Account for capacity realistically — holidays, meetings, support, and unexpected work.
Do not over-commit — it is better to finish early and pull more work than to carry over.
Identify dependencies early in the sprint and resolve them proactively.
The plan is a forecast, not a contract — adapt as you learn during the sprint.
commonMistakes: Over-committing by ignoring capacity constraints.
Not having a clear sprint goal, making the sprint feel like a random collection of tasks.
Not accounting for support duties, meetings, and other non-sprint work.
Treating the sprint plan as immutable rather than adapting to new information.
Not identifying dependencies until they block progress mid-sprint.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government agile delivery, sprint plans should align with GDS service phases and upcoming milestones (service assessments, governance reviews). Sprint goals should connect to user needs identified through research. For teams working across multiple government services, sprint plans help manage shared resource allocation.

artifacts.name: Release Plan
artifacts.description: A plan describing what will be released to users and when, including the scope of each release, deployment approach, rollback strategy, and communication plan for the release.
artifacts.purpose: The release plan coordinates the delivery of working software to users, ensuring that releases are planned, communicated, and executed safely. It manages stakeholder expectations about when features will be available and ensures operational readiness.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during beta when planning the cadence of releases to users. Update as scope and timelines evolve. Essential for coordinating with operations, communications, and support teams.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the release strategy: continuous delivery (every sprint), scheduled releases (monthly/quarterly), or feature-based releases. The strategy should balance user value delivery speed with operational risk.

For each planned release, define the scope (which features/stories), the target date, and any dependencies (infrastructure changes, third-party integrations, communications).

Document the deployment approach: blue-green, canary, rolling update, or big-bang. Include the rollback strategy for each release.

Plan communications: who needs to know about the release, when, and what message? Include internal teams, users, and support staff.

Define release criteria: what must be true before a release proceeds? This typically includes test results, performance benchmarks, and operational readiness.
tips: Release early and often — smaller releases carry less risk than big-bang releases.
Always have a rollback plan — assume every release might need to be reversed.
Communicate releases to support teams before users, so they can handle queries.
Use feature flags to decouple deployment from release — deploy dark, then enable.
Track release metrics: deployment frequency, lead time, failure rate, recovery time.
commonMistakes: Planning releases too far in advance with too much scope, creating big-bang risk.
Not having a tested rollback plan for each release.
Not communicating releases to support and operations teams in advance.
Coupling deployment with release — deploy and release should be independent activities.
Not tracking release metrics to identify improvement opportunities.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, releases to public-facing services should be coordinated with departmental communications teams. Major releases may need ministerial awareness. For services in public beta, releases should be communicated to GDS. Release plans should account for change freeze periods (e.g., around elections, major policy announcements). The GDS Service Standard expects teams to demonstrate they can release frequently and safely.

artifacts.name: Backlog (Product Backlog)
artifacts.description: An ordered list of all known work for the product — user stories, bugs, technical debt, and spikes — prioritised by value and maintained by the product owner as the single source of truth for what the team will work on.
artifacts.purpose: The backlog provides a single, prioritised list of work that ensures the team always works on the most valuable thing next. It makes all known work visible, supports planning, and provides transparency to stakeholders about what is coming and what is not.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create at the start of alpha and maintain throughout the project lifecycle. Refine continuously — the top of the backlog should always be ready for the next sprint. The backlog is never complete; it evolves as understanding grows.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the user needs identified in discovery. Express each as a user story or epic. Add technical enablers, spikes, and known technical debt.

Prioritise ruthlessly — the top items should be the most valuable things to deliver next. Use techniques like MoSCoW, WSJF (Weighted Shortest Job First), or value/effort matrices.

Refine the top of the backlog continuously — stories entering the next sprint should have clear acceptance criteria, estimates, and no unresolved dependencies.

Keep the backlog visible and transparent — stakeholders should be able to see what is planned and what is not. Use the backlog to manage expectations.

Regularly groom the bottom of the backlog — remove items that are no longer relevant. A backlog with hundreds of stale items is not useful.
tips: The backlog is ordered, not just categorised — position matters.
Only the top 2-3 sprints worth of stories need to be fully refined.
Include technical debt and enablers alongside user stories — they compete for priority.
Review and prune regularly — stale items at the bottom add noise without value.
Make the backlog visible to stakeholders to manage expectations transparently.
commonMistakes: Letting the backlog grow indefinitely without pruning stale items.
Not refining stories before they enter a sprint, causing mid-sprint confusion.
Treating all items as equal priority rather than making hard prioritisation decisions.
Hiding technical debt in a separate list rather than making it compete for priority.
Not making the backlog visible to stakeholders, creating expectation mismatches.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the backlog should trace back to validated user needs (GDS Service Standard point 1). Accessibility requirements should be embedded in stories, not treated as a separate backlog. For services in beta, the backlog should include items addressing service assessment recommendations. Technical debt from alpha prototyping should be explicitly captured and prioritised.

artifacts.name: Retrospective Output
artifacts.description: The documented output of a team retrospective — what went well, what did not go well, and what actions the team will take to improve, captured at the end of each sprint or iteration.
artifacts.purpose: Retrospectives drive continuous improvement by creating a regular space for the team to reflect on their process and practices. The documented output ensures that improvement actions are tracked and actually implemented rather than forgotten.
artifacts.whenToUse: Conduct at the end of every sprint. Also conduct after significant events (incidents, releases, assessments). Document the output and track actions to completion.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Facilitate a retrospective using a chosen format (Start/Stop/Continue, 4Ls, Sailboat, Timeline, etc.). Create a safe space where team members can be honest.

Capture observations in categories: what went well (continue doing), what did not go well (stop or change), and what to try (experiments for next sprint).

Prioritise — the team cannot fix everything at once. Select 2-3 actions maximum for the next sprint. Assign owners and make actions specific and achievable.

Track actions from previous retrospectives — did we actually do what we said we would? Celebrate improvements and acknowledge when actions did not work.

Vary the retrospective format to keep it fresh and surface different insights.
tips: Create psychological safety — people must feel safe to be honest without blame.
Limit actions to 2-3 per sprint — too many actions means none get done.
Track actions visibly — put them on the team board alongside sprint work.
Vary the format to prevent retrospective fatigue.
Celebrate improvements — acknowledge when things get better because of retro actions.
commonMistakes: Not creating a safe environment, so people avoid raising real issues.
Identifying too many actions that never get completed.
Not tracking actions from previous retrospectives.
Always using the same format, leading to stale conversations.
Skipping retrospectives when the team is busy — this is when they are most needed.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, retrospective outputs contribute to lessons learned for the programme and can be referenced in GDS service assessments as evidence of continuous improvement (Service Standard point 5). They demonstrate that the team is iterating based on feedback. For cross-government teams, retrospectives help surface collaboration challenges between departments.

artifacts.name: Burndown/Burnup Chart
artifacts.description: A visual chart showing the progress of work completion over time — burndown shows remaining work decreasing towards zero, while burnup shows completed work increasing towards the total scope.
artifacts.purpose: Burndown and burnup charts provide at-a-glance visibility of sprint or release progress, helping teams and stakeholders understand whether delivery is on track. They surface problems early when the trend line diverges from the ideal.
artifacts.whenToUse: Maintain throughout each sprint (sprint burndown) and across the release (release burnup). Update daily. Use at standups and sprint reviews to communicate progress.
artifacts.howToBuild:
For a sprint burndown: plot the total story points committed on day 1, then track remaining points daily as stories are completed. Draw an ideal burndown line from total to zero for comparison.

For a release burnup: plot total scope (top line) and completed work (bottom line) over time. The gap between them shows remaining work. If the scope line rises, scope is being added.

Update daily — the chart loses value if it is only updated at sprint boundaries. Automate if possible using your project management tool.

Analyse the shape: flat periods indicate blocked work, steep drops indicate batch completion (stories not being broken down small enough), and scope line increases indicate scope creep.

Use the chart to forecast: if the current trend continues, when will the work be complete?
tips: Automate chart generation from your project management tool if possible.
Use burnup for releases (shows scope changes) and burndown for sprints.
Flat lines on a burndown indicate blocked work — investigate immediately.
The chart is a conversation starter, not a judgement tool — use it to identify problems, not blame.
Compare actual vs ideal to spot trends early, before they become critical.
commonMistakes: Only updating the chart at sprint boundaries rather than daily.
Using burndown for releases where scope changes — burnup is better for this.
Treating the chart as a performance metric rather than a diagnostic tool.
Not investigating flat periods that indicate blocked work.
Ignoring scope changes that make the burndown misleading.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government agile delivery, burndown/burnup charts provide evidence of delivery progress for governance boards and service assessments. They demonstrate that the team is delivering iteratively and can forecast completion. For GDS assessments, they show that the team is working in an agile way with regular delivery cadence.

artifacts.name: Threat Model
artifacts.description: A structured analysis of potential security threats to a system, identifying threat actors, attack vectors, vulnerabilities, and the controls needed to mitigate risks to an acceptable level.
artifacts.purpose: Threat modelling proactively identifies security risks before they are exploited, enabling the team to design appropriate controls into the architecture rather than bolting them on later. It prioritises security investment based on actual risk rather than generic checklists.
artifacts.whenToUse: Conduct during alpha when the architecture is being designed, and update during beta as the design evolves. Repeat when significant changes are made to the system boundary, data flows, or technology stack.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with a data flow diagram showing how data moves through the system, crossing trust boundaries. Identify where sensitive data is processed, stored, and transmitted.

Identify threat actors: who might want to attack this system and why? Consider external attackers, malicious insiders, nation states, and accidental threats.

Use STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) to systematically identify threats at each component and data flow.

For each identified threat, assess the risk (likelihood × impact) and define controls to mitigate it. Controls may be preventive, detective, or corrective.

Document residual risk — what risk remains after controls are applied? Is this acceptable given the data classification and business context?
tips: Use data flow diagrams as the basis — they make trust boundaries and data movement visible.
Focus on the most valuable assets and most likely threat actors first.
Involve developers in threat modelling — they understand the implementation details.
Update the threat model when the architecture changes significantly.
Use STRIDE as a systematic framework to avoid missing threat categories.
commonMistakes: Treating threat modelling as a one-time activity rather than ongoing.
Not involving developers who understand the implementation details.
Focusing only on external threats and ignoring insider threats.
Identifying threats without defining specific, implementable controls.
Not prioritising — trying to mitigate every conceivable threat equally.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, threat modelling should align with NCSC guidance and the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF). For systems handling OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE or above, threat modelling is expected as part of security accreditation. The threat model should consider nation-state threat actors for government systems. Reference the NCSC's threat intelligence and the government's security classification policy.

artifacts.name: Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)
artifacts.description: A systematic assessment of how personal data processing operations may affect the privacy of individuals, identifying risks and the measures needed to mitigate them, as required by UK GDPR for high-risk processing.
artifacts.purpose: DPIAs ensure that privacy risks are identified and mitigated before processing begins, demonstrating compliance with UK GDPR's accountability principle. They protect individuals' rights and help organisations avoid regulatory action from the ICO.
artifacts.whenToUse: Conduct when planning any new processing of personal data that is likely to result in high risk to individuals. This includes large-scale processing, new technologies, profiling, and processing of special category data. Start in discovery, complete in alpha.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Describe the processing: what personal data will be collected, from whom, for what purpose, how it will be processed, stored, shared, and retained. Be specific and comprehensive.

Assess necessity and proportionality: is the processing necessary for the stated purpose? Could the same outcome be achieved with less data or less intrusive processing?

Identify risks to individuals: what could go wrong? Consider data breaches, inaccurate data, excessive collection, lack of transparency, and inability to exercise rights.

Assess the likelihood and severity of each risk. Define measures to mitigate risks: technical controls (encryption, access control), organisational measures (policies, training), and contractual safeguards.

Consult with the DPO and, if residual risk remains high, consult with the ICO before processing begins.
tips: Start the DPIA early — it should inform design decisions, not just document them after the fact.
Involve the DPO from the beginning, not just for sign-off at the end.
Be specific about data items — 'personal data' is too vague; list exactly what is collected.
Consider the individual's perspective — what would they expect and what might concern them?
Document your reasoning — the DPIA demonstrates accountability even if risks are low.
commonMistakes: Treating the DPIA as a compliance tick-box rather than a genuine privacy analysis.
Starting the DPIA too late, after design decisions have already been made.
Being vague about what personal data is processed and why.
Not considering the individual's perspective and expectations.
Not consulting the DPO or doing so only at the end for rubber-stamping.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, DPIAs are mandatory for new processing likely to result in high risk. The ICO provides specific guidance for public authorities. Government departments must consider the public sector equality duty alongside privacy. DPIAs should reference the lawful basis for processing (often 'public task' for government services) and any relevant legislation (e.g., Digital Economy Act 2017 for data sharing). The Government Data Ethics Framework should also be considered.

artifacts.name: Security Architecture Document
artifacts.description: A document describing the security controls, mechanisms, and design patterns implemented across the solution to protect against identified threats and meet security requirements.
artifacts.purpose: The security architecture ensures that security is designed into the solution systematically rather than added as an afterthought. It provides a comprehensive view of how the system is protected and demonstrates due diligence for security accreditation.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during alpha alongside the solution architecture. Update during beta as security controls are implemented and tested. Required for security accreditation of systems handling sensitive data.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the security requirements derived from data classification, threat model, and regulatory obligations. Define the security posture the system must achieve.

Document the security architecture across layers: network security (firewalls, segmentation, WAF), identity and access management (authentication, authorisation, federation), data protection (encryption, tokenisation, masking), application security (input validation, output encoding, session management), and operational security (logging, monitoring, incident response).

For each security control, document: what threat it mitigates, how it is implemented, how it is monitored, and how its effectiveness is verified.

Show security boundaries and trust zones on architecture diagrams. Document how data is protected as it crosses boundaries.

Include the security testing approach: SAST, DAST, penetration testing, and security monitoring in production.
tips: Align security controls with identified threats from the threat model — every control should mitigate a specific risk.
Use defence in depth — do not rely on a single control for any threat.
Document both preventive and detective controls — you need to know when attacks occur.
Include operational security — how will security be maintained in production?
Reference NCSC guidance for government-specific security patterns.
commonMistakes: Listing security controls without linking them to specific threats or risks.
Focusing only on perimeter security and neglecting application-level controls.
Not documenting how security controls are monitored and verified.
Treating security architecture as static — it must evolve with the threat landscape.
Not including operational security (monitoring, incident response, patching).
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, security architecture must align with NCSC cloud security principles and the Cyber Assessment Framework (CAF). Systems handling OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE data require specific controls documented in the security architecture. The architecture should reference the government's zero-trust network architecture principles and demonstrate compliance with Cyber Essentials Plus. For systems connecting to PSN or other government networks, specific connectivity security requirements apply.

artifacts.name: Information Asset Register
artifacts.description: A catalogue of all information assets held by the organisation or system, documenting their classification, owner, location, access controls, and retention requirements.
artifacts.purpose: The information asset register provides visibility of what data the organisation holds, where it is, who is responsible for it, and how it is protected. It supports data protection compliance, security management, and information governance.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery when identifying what data the system will process. Maintain throughout the system lifecycle as new data assets are introduced or retired.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Identify all information assets: databases, file stores, documents, emails, backups, and any other repositories of information. Include both digital and physical assets.

For each asset, document: what it contains, its security classification, the Information Asset Owner (IAO), where it is stored, who has access, how it is protected, and its retention period.

Assess the risk for each asset: what would happen if it were disclosed, modified, or lost? This drives the security controls required.

Map data flows between assets to understand how information moves and where it might be at risk during transit.

Review regularly — at least annually or when significant changes occur to the system or data landscape.
tips: Assign a named Information Asset Owner for every asset — accountability must be personal.
Include data in transit and temporary stores, not just permanent databases.
Link to the DPIA for assets containing personal data.
Use the register to drive access reviews — who has access and do they still need it?
Keep it simple and maintainable — an overly complex register will not be kept up to date.
commonMistakes: Only registering databases and forgetting about file shares, emails, and backups.
Not assigning clear ownership for each asset.
Creating the register once and never updating it.
Not linking the register to access control reviews.
Making it too granular — register at the right level of abstraction.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, Information Asset Registers are required under the Government Security Policy Framework. Each department must have a Senior Information Risk Owner (SIRO) who oversees information risk. IAOs are responsible for their assets and must complete annual risk assessments. The register supports compliance with UK GDPR's accountability principle and the government's security classification policy (OFFICIAL, SECRET, TOP SECRET).

artifacts.name: Risk Treatment Plan
artifacts.description: A plan documenting how identified security risks will be treated — whether through mitigation, transfer, avoidance, or acceptance — with specific actions, owners, timelines, and success criteria for each treatment.
artifacts.purpose: The risk treatment plan translates risk assessment findings into concrete actions, ensuring that identified risks are actively managed rather than just documented. It provides accountability and tracking for risk reduction activities.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create after completing a risk assessment or threat model. Update as treatments are implemented and new risks are identified. Review at security governance meetings.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the risk assessment output — the list of identified risks with their likelihood, impact, and current risk score.

For each risk, select a treatment strategy: mitigate (reduce likelihood or impact), transfer (insurance or contractual), avoid (change approach to eliminate the risk), or accept (acknowledge and monitor).

For risks being mitigated, define specific controls or actions that will reduce the risk. Specify: what will be done, who is responsible, by when, what resources are needed, and how success will be measured.

Calculate the target residual risk after treatment — is this within the organisation's risk appetite? If not, additional treatment is needed.

Track implementation progress and verify effectiveness through testing or audit.
tips: Not all risks need mitigation — some should be accepted if the cost of treatment exceeds the risk.
Define measurable success criteria for each treatment — how will you know it worked?
Prioritise treatments by risk score — address the highest risks first.
Include the cost of treatment — risk management is about proportionate investment.
Review treatment effectiveness periodically — controls can degrade over time.
commonMistakes: Treating all risks the same rather than prioritising by score and appetite.
Defining vague treatments without specific actions, owners, or timelines.
Not verifying that treatments actually reduce risk as intended.
Accepting risks without proper authority — risk acceptance needs senior sign-off.
Not reviewing treatment effectiveness over time.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, risk treatment plans should align with the Government Security Policy Framework and NCSC guidance. Risk acceptance decisions above certain thresholds require SIRO approval. For systems handling sensitive data, the risk treatment plan forms part of the security accreditation evidence. artifacts.name: Data Model (Logical/Physical)
artifacts.description: A structured representation of the data entities, their attributes, relationships, and constraints within a system — logical models show business concepts independent of technology, while physical models specify database implementation details.
artifacts.purpose: Data models ensure that data is structured correctly to support business requirements, maintain integrity, and enable efficient querying. They provide a shared understanding of data semantics between business and technical stakeholders.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create the logical model during alpha when understanding the domain. Create the physical model during beta when implementing the database. Update as the data requirements evolve.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the logical model: identify the key business entities (nouns in the domain). For each entity, define its attributes and their data types. Identify relationships between entities (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many).

Validate the logical model against business requirements — can it support all the required queries and operations? Walk through user stories to verify.

Translate to a physical model: map entities to tables, choose specific data types, define primary and foreign keys, add indexes for query performance, and specify constraints.

Document data validation rules, default values, and business rules that the data model enforces. Include data lifecycle considerations: how is data created, updated, archived, and deleted?

Consider data migration if replacing an existing system — how will data be mapped from the old model to the new?
tips: Start with the logical model — do not jump straight to physical tables.
Normalise to 3NF for transactional data, then denormalise deliberately for performance where needed.
Document the reasoning behind denormalisation decisions.
Include audit fields (created_at, updated_at, created_by) from the start.
Consider GDPR requirements — can personal data be easily identified and deleted?
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to physical design without understanding the logical domain model.
Over-normalising to the point where queries become impractically complex.
Not considering query patterns when designing indexes.
Forgetting audit and soft-delete requirements until late in development.
Not planning for data migration from legacy systems.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, data models should align with cross-government data standards where they exist (e.g., address formats, person names). Consider the Government Data Quality Framework when defining validation rules. For services processing personal data, the model should support GDPR rights (right to erasure, data portability). Reference the cross-government data architecture principles published by CDDO.

artifacts.name: Data Dictionary
artifacts.description: A comprehensive reference document defining every data element in the system — its name, definition, data type, valid values, source, owner, and any business rules or constraints that apply.
artifacts.purpose: The data dictionary eliminates ambiguity about what data means, ensuring consistent interpretation across teams. It supports data quality, integration design, and regulatory compliance by providing a single authoritative definition for each data element.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create alongside the data model during alpha. Maintain throughout the project as new data elements are introduced. Essential for integration design and data migration.
artifacts.howToBuild:
For each data element in the system, document: its business name, technical name, definition (in plain English), data type, format, valid values or ranges, source system, owner, and any validation rules.

Group elements by entity or domain area for easy navigation. Include cross-references to related elements.

Document derivation rules for calculated fields — how is the value computed and from what source data?

Include data quality rules: what constitutes valid data? What are the mandatory fields? What are the referential integrity constraints?

Keep the dictionary in sync with the actual implementation — it should reflect reality, not aspirations.
tips: Use plain English definitions that business stakeholders can understand.
Include examples of valid and invalid values for each element.
Document the authoritative source for each data element.
Keep it in sync with the code — automate generation from schema where possible.
Include data classification (personal data, sensitive, public) for each element.
commonMistakes: Writing definitions that are circular or use technical jargon business users cannot understand.
Not keeping the dictionary in sync with the actual database schema.
Omitting validation rules, leading to inconsistent data quality.
Not documenting the authoritative source, causing confusion about which system is correct.
Making it too granular or too high-level — find the right balance.

artifacts.purpose: The data flow map provides end-to-end visibility of data movement, supporting data governance, privacy compliance, security analysis, and operational understanding. It answers the question: where does our data go?
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery when understanding the data landscape. Update when new data flows are introduced or existing ones change. Essential for DPIAs and security assessments.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Identify all data sources: user inputs, external system feeds, file imports, API calls, and manual data entry points.

Trace each data flow through the system: where does data go after it enters? What transformations occur? Where is it stored? Who can access it at each point?

Map data outputs: reports, API responses, file exports, notifications, and downstream system feeds. Include both automated and manual data movements.

Highlight personal data flows specifically — these are critical for GDPR compliance and DPIA purposes.

Document data volumes, frequencies, and latency requirements for each flow to support capacity planning.
tips: Use different colours or line styles for different data classifications.
Show both automated and manual data flows — manual processes are often overlooked.
Include data at rest (storage) as well as data in motion (flows).
Highlight cross-boundary flows (between organisations, security zones, or jurisdictions).
Keep it at the right level of abstraction — too detailed and it becomes unreadable.
commonMistakes: Only showing automated flows and missing manual data handling processes.
Not showing data classification, making security analysis impossible.
Making the map too detailed for a single diagram — use levels of decomposition.
Not updating the map when new flows are introduced.
Forgetting about backup and disaster recovery data flows.

artifacts.name: Data Sharing Agreement
artifacts.description: A formal agreement between two or more organisations defining the terms under which personal or sensitive data will be shared, including purposes, safeguards, responsibilities, and legal basis.
artifacts.purpose: Data sharing agreements ensure that data is shared lawfully, securely, and with clear accountability. They protect individuals' rights, define each party's responsibilities, and provide a legal framework for the data exchange.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create before any sharing of personal data between organisations begins. Required when integrating with other government departments, third-party suppliers, or partner organisations that will access personal data.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the parties to the agreement and their roles (controller, processor, joint controller). Specify the legal basis for sharing under UK GDPR.

Describe precisely what data will be shared: data elements, data subjects, volume, and frequency. Be specific — vague descriptions create compliance risk.

Define the purpose limitation: what can the receiving party use the data for? What are they prohibited from doing?

Specify security requirements: how must the data be protected in transit and at rest? What access controls are required? How will breaches be reported?

Include retention and deletion requirements, individual rights handling, audit rights, and termination provisions.
tips: Be specific about what data is shared — vague agreements create compliance risk.
Define clear responsibilities for handling data subject rights requests.
Include breach notification requirements with specific timelines.
Specify audit rights so you can verify the other party's compliance.
Set a review date — agreements should not run indefinitely without review.
commonMistakes: Being vague about what data is shared, creating scope for misuse.
Not specifying the legal basis for sharing under UK GDPR.
Omitting breach notification requirements and timelines.
Not including termination provisions and data return/deletion requirements.
Failing to specify how data subject rights requests will be handled across parties.

artifacts.name: Data Quality Assessment
artifacts.description: An assessment of the quality of data within a system or dataset, measuring dimensions such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, and validity against defined quality standards.
artifacts.purpose: Data quality assessments identify problems with data that could affect service delivery, decision-making, or compliance. They provide a baseline for improvement and help prioritise data cleansing and quality improvement activities.
artifacts.whenToUse: Conduct during discovery when assessing legacy data for migration. Repeat periodically in live to monitor ongoing data quality. Essential before major data migrations or integrations.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the data quality dimensions relevant to your context: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness, and integrity.

For each dimension, define measurable quality rules. For example: 'Email addresses must match valid format' (validity), 'All mandatory fields must be populated' (completeness), 'Status values must be from the approved list' (consistency).

Profile the data: run the quality rules against the actual data and measure the pass/fail rates. Use automated data profiling tools where possible.

Analyse the results: where are the quality issues? What is the root cause? What is the business impact of poor quality?

Define improvement actions: data cleansing for existing issues, validation rules to prevent future issues, and monitoring to detect quality degradation.
tips: Define quality rules with business stakeholders — they understand what good data looks like.
Automate quality checks so they run continuously, not just as one-off assessments.
Focus on data that matters most to the service — not all data quality issues are equal.
Track quality metrics over time to show improvement trends.
Address root causes, not just symptoms — fix the process that creates bad data.
commonMistakes: Assessing quality without defined rules, making results subjective.
Not involving business stakeholders in defining what good quality means.
Treating data quality as a one-time activity rather than ongoing monitoring.
Focusing on symptoms (bad data) without addressing root causes (bad processes).
Not prioritising — trying to fix all quality issues at once rather than focusing on impact.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the Government Data Quality Framework provides guidance on assessing and improving data quality. Poor data quality in government services can lead to incorrect decisions affecting citizens. For data migration from legacy systems, quality assessment is essential to avoid migrating garbage. artifacts.name: Service Blueprint
artifacts.description: A diagram showing the end-to-end service delivery from the user's perspective, including frontstage interactions (what users see), backstage processes (what staff do), and support processes (systems and infrastructure that enable delivery).
artifacts.purpose: Service blueprints reveal the full complexity of service delivery by showing the relationship between user-facing touchpoints and the behind-the-scenes processes that support them. They identify pain points, inefficiencies, and opportunities for improvement across the entire service chain.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery to understand the current service (as-is) and during alpha to design the future service (to-be). Update as the service design evolves through beta.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the user journey — what steps does the user take from first awareness of the service through to completion? Map these as the top layer of the blueprint.

Below the line of interaction, map the frontstage actions — what do service staff do that the user can see? Phone calls, emails, face-to-face interactions.

Below the line of visibility, map backstage actions — what do staff do that the user cannot see? Processing, checking, decision-making.

Below the line of internal interaction, map support processes — what systems, databases, and infrastructure enable the backstage actions?

Identify pain points, wait times, and failure points at each stage. Annotate with metrics where available.
tips: Start with the user's perspective and work downward — the user journey drives everything else.
Include time indicators — how long does each step take? Where are the delays?
Mark pain points and failure points clearly — these are improvement opportunities.
Show both digital and non-digital touchpoints — most services are not purely digital.
Validate the blueprint with frontline staff — they know the reality of service delivery.
commonMistakes: Only mapping the digital journey and ignoring offline touchpoints.
Not including the support systems layer, hiding technical dependencies.
Making the blueprint too detailed for a single diagram — use swimlanes and keep it readable.
Not validating with frontline staff who actually deliver the service.
Creating a to-be blueprint without understanding the as-is first.

artifacts.name: User Journey Map
artifacts.description: A visual representation of the steps a user takes to accomplish a goal with the service, including their actions, thoughts, emotions, pain points, and touchpoints at each stage of the journey.
artifacts.purpose: User journey maps build empathy by showing the service from the user's perspective, revealing emotional highs and lows, pain points, and moments of truth. They help teams prioritise improvements that have the greatest impact on user experience.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery based on user research findings. Refine during alpha as the team learns more about user behaviour. Use to communicate user needs to stakeholders and guide design decisions.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Base the journey map on real user research — interviews, observations, and usability testing. Do not invent journeys based on assumptions.

Define the persona taking this journey — who is this user, what is their context, and what is their goal?

Map the stages of the journey from the user's perspective: awareness, consideration, action, completion, and aftercare. For each stage, document what the user does, thinks, and feels.

Identify touchpoints at each stage — where does the user interact with the service? Include all channels (web, phone, post, face-to-face).

Mark pain points (frustrations, confusion, delays) and moments of delight. Rate the emotional experience at each stage to create an emotion curve.
tips: Base journey maps on real research, not assumptions — validate with actual users.
Include the emotional dimension — how users feel matters as much as what they do.
Show the journey before and after the digital service — users do not start at your homepage.
Create separate maps for different personas — their journeys may differ significantly.
Use the map to identify the biggest pain points and prioritise improvements.
commonMistakes: Creating journey maps based on assumptions rather than research.
Only mapping the happy path and ignoring error scenarios and edge cases.
Starting the journey at the service homepage rather than the user's actual starting point.
Not including emotions and pain points, reducing the map to a process flow.
Creating beautiful maps that are never used to drive design decisions.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, user journey maps are key evidence for GDS service assessments (Service Standard point 1: understand users and their needs). They should be based on research with real users, including those with access needs. Journey maps should cover the whole service, not just the digital part — including offline channels and assisted digital paths. GDS expects teams to show how journey maps informed design decisions.

artifacts.name: Persona Document
artifacts.description: A research-based representation of a key user group, describing their characteristics, goals, behaviours, needs, pain points, and context, used to keep the team focused on real user needs throughout design and development.
artifacts.purpose: Personas make abstract user groups concrete and relatable, helping teams make design decisions with specific users in mind. They prevent the team from designing for themselves and ensure diverse user needs are considered.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery based on user research. Reference throughout alpha and beta when making design decisions. Update as research reveals new insights about users.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Base personas on real user research — interviews, surveys, and observation. Identify patterns in user behaviour, needs, and characteristics that define distinct user groups.

For each persona, document: a name and photo (fictional but representative), demographic context, goals and motivations, behaviours and habits, pain points and frustrations, technology usage, and accessibility needs.

Include a scenario or quote that brings the persona to life — something that captures their essence and makes them memorable.

Keep the number of personas manageable — 3-5 primary personas is typical. More than that and the team cannot keep them all in mind.

Validate personas with the team and stakeholders — do they recognise these users? Do they ring true?
tips: Base personas on research, not assumptions — they must represent real user groups.
Include accessibility needs and digital confidence levels.
Keep personas visible — print them and put them on the wall.
Reference personas in user stories and design discussions.
Update personas as you learn more through ongoing research.
commonMistakes: Creating personas based on assumptions rather than research.
Making personas too detailed with irrelevant personal information.
Creating too many personas that the team cannot remember.
Not including accessibility needs and diverse user characteristics.
Creating personas and then never referencing them in design decisions.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, personas should reflect the diversity of the UK population, including users with access needs, low digital confidence, and those using assisted digital channels. GDS expects personas to be research-based and referenced in service assessments. Include users who may need support (e.g., those with cognitive disabilities, non-native English speakers, users in rural areas with poor connectivity).

artifacts.name: As-Is / To-Be Process Map
artifacts.description: A visual representation of a business process showing the sequence of activities, decision points, roles involved, and handoffs — created for both the current state (as-is) and the desired future state (to-be) to show the improvement.
artifacts.purpose: Process maps make complex processes visible and understandable, revealing inefficiencies, bottlenecks, and unnecessary steps. Comparing as-is with to-be demonstrates the value of change and guides implementation.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create the as-is map during discovery to understand current processes. Create the to-be map during alpha to design improved processes. Use the comparison to build the business case for change.
artifacts.howToBuild:
For the as-is map: observe and document the current process through interviews with staff, shadowing, and document review. Include all steps, decision points, handoffs, and wait times — even unofficial workarounds.

Use standard notation (BPMN is recommended): rectangles for activities, diamonds for decisions, circles for start/end, and swimlanes for different roles or systems.

Annotate with metrics: how long does each step take? Where are the bottlenecks? What is the error rate? Where do things go wrong?

For the to-be map: redesign the process to eliminate waste, reduce handoffs, automate where possible, and improve the user experience. Show what changes and what stays the same.

Quantify the improvement: how much time/cost/effort is saved? What quality improvements are expected?
tips: Map the real process, not the official process — they are often different.
Include wait times between steps — these are often where most time is spent.
Use swimlanes to show handoffs between roles or teams clearly.
Validate the as-is map with the people who actually do the work.
Quantify improvements in the to-be map to support the business case.
commonMistakes: Mapping the official process rather than what actually happens in practice.
Not including wait times and delays between process steps.
Making the map too detailed, obscuring the key flow and decision points.
Not validating with frontline staff who execute the process daily.
Creating a to-be map that is unrealistic or ignores real constraints.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, process maps support the GDS principle of understanding the whole service. They help identify where digital transformation can eliminate manual steps and reduce processing times. For services that span multiple departments, process maps reveal the handoffs that cause delays. They support business cases for digital investment by quantifying current inefficiency.

artifacts.name: Service Level Agreement (SLA)
artifacts.description: A formal agreement defining the expected level of service between a provider and consumer, including availability targets, performance metrics, support response times, and the consequences of not meeting agreed levels.
artifacts.purpose: SLAs set clear expectations for service quality, provide a basis for measuring performance, and define accountability when service levels are not met. They protect both providers and consumers by making expectations explicit and measurable.
artifacts.whenToUse: Define during beta when the service is approaching live operation. Agree with stakeholders before go-live. Review annually or when service characteristics change significantly.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the services covered by the SLA — what exactly is being provided and to whom? Be specific about scope and boundaries.

Set measurable service level targets for key metrics: availability, performance, capacity, and support response times. Base targets on user needs and business requirements, not arbitrary numbers.

Define how metrics will be measured: what tools, what measurement points, what reporting frequency? Ensure measurement is objective and automated where possible.

Specify exclusions: planned maintenance windows, force majeure, and any conditions under which the SLA does not apply.

Define the review and escalation process: how often is performance reviewed? What happens when targets are missed? What are the consequences?
tips: Base SLA targets on user needs, not technical convenience.
Define how metrics are measured — ambiguous measurement leads to disputes.
Include both availability and performance targets — a service can be available but unusably slow.
Set realistic targets — 99.99% availability is very different from 99.9% in practice.
Review SLAs regularly — user expectations and service capabilities change over time.
commonMistakes: Setting arbitrary targets without understanding user needs or cost implications.
Not defining how metrics are measured, leading to disputes about whether targets are met.
Setting targets that are unrealistically high, guaranteeing failure.
Not including exclusions for planned maintenance, making maintenance impossible.
Not defining consequences for missed targets, making the SLA toothless.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, SLAs should align with the GDS Service Standard expectation of reliable, performant services. Government services typically target 99.9% availability during business hours. SLAs with suppliers should be managed through the contract and aligned with the Government Commercial Function standards. For shared platforms, SLAs should reference the platform provider's commitments (e.g., AWS SLA for underlying services).
