artifacts.name: Runbook / Playbook
artifacts.description: A collection of documented procedures for operating, maintaining, and troubleshooting a service in production, providing step-by-step instructions for common operational tasks and incident response scenarios.
artifacts.purpose: Runbooks enable operations teams to manage services consistently and effectively, reducing reliance on individual knowledge. They accelerate incident response, ensure consistent procedures, and support on-call engineers who may not be familiar with every service detail.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during beta as the service approaches production readiness. Update continuously as new operational scenarios are encountered. Essential for operations handover and on-call support.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Identify all operational scenarios: routine tasks (deployments, backups, scaling), common issues (high CPU, disk full, connection errors), and incident response procedures.

For each scenario, write step-by-step instructions that someone unfamiliar with the service could follow. Include: what triggers this procedure, what tools are needed, exact commands to run, expected outputs, and what to do if something goes wrong.

Include diagnostic procedures: how to check service health, how to identify the root cause of common symptoms, and how to gather information for escalation.

Document escalation paths: when should the on-call engineer escalate? To whom? What information should they provide?

Keep runbooks close to the code — store them in the repository and update them when the service changes.
tips: Write for someone who has never seen this service before — they may be on-call at 3am.
Include exact commands, not just descriptions of what to do.
Test runbook procedures regularly — untested procedures may not work when needed.
Include rollback procedures for every change procedure.
Keep runbooks in version control alongside the code they document.
commonMistakes: Writing vague procedures that require prior knowledge to follow.
Not keeping runbooks updated when the service changes.
Not testing procedures — they may be outdated or incorrect.
Making runbooks too long — separate into focused procedures, not one massive document.
Not including escalation criteria and contact information.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, runbooks support the GDS Service Standard requirement for operational readiness (point 14). They are essential for services transitioning from project delivery to business-as-usual operations. For services managed by third-party suppliers, runbooks define the operational procedures the supplier must follow. They support the government's service continuity requirements.

artifacts.name: Incident Response Plan
artifacts.description: A documented plan defining how the team will detect, respond to, communicate about, and recover from service incidents, including roles, procedures, communication templates, and post-incident review processes.
artifacts.purpose: The incident response plan ensures that when things go wrong, the team responds quickly, consistently, and effectively. It reduces mean time to recovery, ensures appropriate communication, and supports learning from incidents to prevent recurrence.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create before the service goes live. Test through incident simulations (game days). Update after real incidents based on lessons learned.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define incident severity levels with clear criteria for each level. What constitutes a P1 (critical) vs P2 (high) vs P3 (medium) incident?

Define roles during an incident: Incident Commander (coordinates response), Technical Lead (drives resolution), Communications Lead (manages stakeholder updates), and Scribe (documents timeline and actions).

Document the response process: detection (how incidents are identified), triage (severity assessment), response (who is called, what actions are taken), communication (who is told what and when), resolution (how the service is restored), and review (post-incident learning).

Create communication templates for different audiences: technical teams, service owners, senior leadership, and users. Pre-written templates save critical time during incidents.

Plan for post-incident reviews: blameless retrospectives that focus on systemic improvements rather than individual blame.
tips: Practice the plan through regular incident simulations (game days).
Keep communication templates pre-written — you do not want to wordsmith during an incident.
Define clear severity criteria so there is no debate about classification during an incident.
Make the plan accessible — on-call engineers need to find it quickly at 3am.
Focus post-incident reviews on systemic improvements, not blame.
commonMistakes: Creating a plan but never practising it through simulations.
Not defining clear severity criteria, leading to debates during incidents.
Forgetting the communication plan — stakeholders need updates during incidents.
Not conducting post-incident reviews, missing opportunities to prevent recurrence.
Making the plan too complex to follow under pressure.

artifacts.name: Disaster Recovery Plan
artifacts.description: A plan documenting how the service will be recovered in the event of a major disaster — data centre failure, region outage, data corruption, or other catastrophic events — including recovery procedures, RTO/RPO targets, and testing approach.
artifacts.purpose: The disaster recovery plan ensures that the service can be restored within acceptable timeframes after a major failure, protecting users and the organisation from extended outages. It provides confidence that the service is resilient to catastrophic events.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during beta as part of operational readiness. Test at least annually through DR exercises. Update when the architecture or infrastructure changes significantly.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define Recovery Time Objective (RTO) — how quickly must the service be restored? And Recovery Point Objective (RPO) — how much data loss is acceptable? These drive the DR strategy and investment.

Document the DR strategy: active-active (multi-region), active-passive (warm standby), pilot light (minimal standby), or backup-restore. The strategy should be proportionate to the RTO/RPO requirements and budget.

Document recovery procedures step by step: what needs to be done, in what order, by whom, using what tools? Include infrastructure provisioning, data restoration, application deployment, and verification.

Define the testing approach: how often will DR be tested? What scenarios will be simulated? How will success be measured?

Include communication procedures during a DR event — who needs to know, what decisions need to be made, and who has authority to invoke the DR plan.
tips: Test the DR plan regularly — an untested plan is not a plan, it is a hope.
Automate recovery procedures where possible — manual steps under pressure are error-prone.
Document dependencies on third-party services and their DR capabilities.
Include data validation steps — restoring corrupted data is worse than no restoration.
Keep the plan accessible outside the primary infrastructure — if the data centre is down, can you access the plan?
commonMistakes: Never testing the DR plan, discovering it does not work during a real disaster.
Setting unrealistic RTO/RPO targets without understanding the cost implications.
Not documenting the recovery procedure in sufficient detail for someone to follow under pressure.
Forgetting about data — infrastructure recovery without data recovery is useless.
Not considering dependencies on third-party services that may also be affected.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, disaster recovery requirements are driven by the Government Security Policy Framework and business continuity obligations. Critical national infrastructure services have specific resilience requirements. The NCSC provides guidance on resilient architectures. DR plans should account for the government's shared infrastructure dependencies and cross-departmental service dependencies. Regular DR testing is expected as part of service assurance.

artifacts.name: Capacity Plan
artifacts.description: A plan documenting current resource utilisation, projected growth, and the actions needed to ensure the service has sufficient capacity to meet demand — covering compute, storage, network, and human resources.
artifacts.purpose: Capacity planning ensures the service can handle expected and unexpected demand without degradation. It prevents both under-provisioning (causing outages) and over-provisioning (wasting money), optimising cost while maintaining service quality.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during beta based on performance testing results. Update quarterly or when significant changes to demand are expected. Review after major traffic events.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Baseline current capacity: what resources are deployed, what is the current utilisation, and what is the headroom? Measure across all resource types: CPU, memory, storage, network, database connections, and API rate limits.

Forecast demand: what growth is expected? Consider organic growth, seasonal patterns, marketing campaigns, and policy changes that might drive traffic spikes.

Model capacity requirements: given the demand forecast, what resources will be needed? Include both steady-state and peak requirements.

Define scaling strategy: auto-scaling policies, manual scaling procedures, and lead times for capacity changes that cannot be automated.

Set monitoring and alerting thresholds: at what utilisation level should alerts fire? What is the trigger for capacity review?
tips: Plan for peak, not average — services fail at peak load, not average load.
Include lead times for capacity changes that cannot be automated (e.g., database scaling).
Monitor trends, not just current values — a slowly filling disk is a future outage.
Account for seasonal patterns in government services (tax deadlines, benefit changes).
Include cost projections — capacity planning should optimise cost as well as performance.
commonMistakes: Planning only for average load and being surprised by peaks.
Not accounting for growth — today's capacity may be insufficient in 6 months.
Ignoring non-compute resources: database connections, API rate limits, storage.
Not testing capacity assumptions through load testing.
Over-provisioning everything without considering cost optimisation.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, capacity planning should account for predictable demand spikes (tax return deadlines, benefit payment dates, policy announcements). Government services may experience sudden traffic surges from media coverage or ministerial announcements. Cloud cost optimisation is important for demonstrating value for money. The Government Digital Service expects services to handle demand gracefully, including through queuing and rate limiting where appropriate.

artifacts.name: Monitoring and Alerting Specification
artifacts.description: A specification defining what metrics, logs, and traces will be collected from the service, what dashboards will be created, what alert thresholds will trigger notifications, and how the team will use observability data to maintain service health.
artifacts.purpose: The monitoring specification ensures that the team has visibility into service health, can detect problems before users are affected, and can diagnose issues quickly when they occur. It transforms operations from reactive to proactive.
artifacts.whenToUse: Define during beta as the service is being built for production. Implement alongside the service code. Refine based on operational experience in live.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the four pillars of observability: metrics (quantitative measurements), logs (event records), traces (request flow through distributed systems), and alerts (notifications when things go wrong).

For metrics: identify the key indicators of service health. Use the RED method (Rate, Errors, Duration) for services and the USE method (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors) for resources.

For logs: define what events to log, at what level, in what format (structured JSON recommended), and where they are stored. Include correlation IDs for tracing requests across services.

For alerts: define thresholds that indicate real problems (not noise). Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting to reduce false positives. Define who is notified and how.

Create dashboards: a service overview dashboard for at-a-glance health, and detailed dashboards for each component for diagnosis.
tips: Alert on symptoms (user-facing impact), not causes (CPU high) — causes without symptoms are not urgent.
Use structured logging (JSON) for easy querying and analysis.
Include correlation IDs in all logs and traces for end-to-end request tracking.
Start with fewer, high-quality alerts rather than many noisy ones.
Create runbook links in alert notifications so responders know what to do immediately.
commonMistakes: Creating too many alerts that cause alert fatigue and get ignored.
Alerting on causes (CPU high) rather than symptoms (error rate high).
Not including correlation IDs, making it impossible to trace requests across services.
Not creating dashboards, forcing engineers to write queries during incidents.
Logging too much (cost) or too little (cannot diagnose issues).
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, monitoring should support the GDS Service Standard requirement for measuring performance (point 14). Key performance indicators should include the 4 mandatory KPIs: cost per transaction, user satisfaction, completion rate, and digital take-up. Monitoring data supports service assessments and operational reviews. Security monitoring should align with NCSC guidance on protective monitoring.

artifacts.name: Statement of Requirements (SoR)
artifacts.description: A document defining what the organisation needs from a supplier — the functional requirements, non-functional requirements, constraints, and evaluation criteria that will be used to assess supplier proposals.
artifacts.purpose: The SoR communicates requirements to the market clearly and consistently, enabling suppliers to propose appropriate solutions. It provides the basis for fair evaluation and ensures the procured solution meets actual needs.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during the procurement planning phase, before going to market. It forms part of the Invitation to Tender (ITT) or Request for Proposal (RFP). Update if requirements change during the procurement process.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the business context: what problem needs solving, who are the users, and what outcomes are required? Suppliers need to understand the why, not just the what.

Define functional requirements: what must the solution do? Group by capability area and prioritise using MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't).

Define non-functional requirements: performance, scalability, security, accessibility, and availability targets. Be specific and measurable.

Specify constraints: technology standards, integration requirements, data residency, security classification, and any mandatory platforms or approaches.

Define evaluation criteria: how will proposals be assessed? What weighting applies to each criterion? This ensures fair and transparent evaluation.
tips: Write requirements as outcomes, not solutions — tell suppliers what you need, not how to build it.
Prioritise clearly using MoSCoW — suppliers need to know what is essential vs desirable.
Include enough context for suppliers to propose innovative solutions.
Make evaluation criteria transparent — suppliers should know how they will be assessed.
Reference government standards (TCoP, Service Standard, WCAG) explicitly.
commonMistakes: Writing requirements as solutions rather than outcomes, constraining supplier innovation.
Not prioritising requirements, implying everything is equally important.
Being too vague for suppliers to estimate effort and cost accurately.
Not including non-functional requirements, getting a solution that works but does not perform.
Making evaluation criteria unclear, leading to challenges from unsuccessful suppliers.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, SoRs should reference the Technology Code of Practice, GDS Service Standard, and relevant government standards. Procurement should use Crown Commercial Service frameworks where possible (G-Cloud, DOS, Technology Services). The SoR should be proportionate to the contract value and follow Government Commercial Function guidance. For digital services, the SoR should require agile delivery and user-centred design approaches.

artifacts.name: Invitation to Tender (ITT) Technical Annex
artifacts.description: The technical section of an Invitation to Tender that specifies the technical requirements, architecture constraints, integration needs, and technical evaluation criteria that suppliers must address in their proposals.
artifacts.purpose: The technical annex ensures that supplier proposals address specific technical requirements and can be evaluated consistently on technical merit. It communicates the technical landscape suppliers will work within and the standards they must meet.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create as part of the ITT package during procurement. It supplements the Statement of Requirements with detailed technical specifications. Review with the technical evaluation panel before publication.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define the technical landscape: what existing systems must the solution integrate with? What platforms and standards are mandated? What is the current architecture context?

Specify technical requirements in detail: API specifications, data formats, security standards, hosting requirements, and development practices expected.

Define the technical evaluation criteria: what technical questions must suppliers answer? How will technical proposals be scored?

Include architecture constraints and preferences: cloud platform, programming languages, frameworks, and patterns that are required or preferred.

Specify deliverables: what technical documentation, source code, and knowledge transfer is expected?
tips: Be specific enough for accurate proposals but flexible enough for supplier innovation.
Include the current architecture context so suppliers understand the integration landscape.
Define technical evaluation questions clearly so proposals are comparable.
Reference government technical standards explicitly.
Include expectations for source code ownership, documentation, and knowledge transfer.
commonMistakes: Being so prescriptive that suppliers cannot propose innovative approaches.
Not providing enough context about the existing technical landscape.
Omitting security and accessibility requirements from the technical annex.
Not defining clear technical evaluation criteria, making scoring subjective.
Forgetting to specify source code ownership and IP rights.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, technical annexes should mandate compliance with the Technology Code of Practice, GDS Service Standard, WCAG 2.2 AA, and NCSC security guidance. They should require use of open standards and open source where appropriate. Source code should be owned by the Crown. Suppliers should demonstrate experience with government digital delivery and GDS service assessments.

artifacts.name: Vendor Assessment Matrix
artifacts.description: A structured evaluation framework for comparing supplier proposals against defined criteria, enabling fair, transparent, and defensible procurement decisions.
artifacts.purpose: The vendor assessment matrix ensures that supplier selection is based on objective criteria rather than subjective preference. It provides an audit trail for the procurement decision and protects against challenge from unsuccessful suppliers.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create before evaluating supplier proposals — the criteria and weightings must be defined before seeing any proposals to ensure fairness. Use during the evaluation period to score and compare proposals.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Define evaluation criteria aligned with the SoR and ITT. Typical categories: technical quality, team and delivery approach, price, and social value.

Assign weightings to each criterion reflecting their relative importance. Weightings must be published in the ITT so suppliers know what matters most.

Define the scoring scale (typically 0-5 or 0-10) with clear descriptors for each score level. What does a 5 look like vs a 3?

Evaluate each proposal independently before comparing. Each evaluator should score independently, then moderate as a panel to reach consensus.

Document the rationale for scores — this is essential for providing feedback to unsuccessful suppliers and defending against challenges.
tips: Define criteria and weightings before seeing any proposals — this ensures fairness.
Use clear scoring descriptors so evaluators apply consistent standards.
Evaluate independently first, then moderate as a panel.
Document rationale for every score — you may need to justify decisions.
Separate price evaluation from quality evaluation to avoid bias.
commonMistakes: Changing criteria or weightings after seeing proposals — this is unfair and potentially illegal.
Not defining clear scoring descriptors, leading to inconsistent scoring.
Not documenting rationale, making it impossible to provide feedback or defend challenges.
Allowing one evaluator to dominate the panel discussion.
Not separating price from quality evaluation.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, vendor assessment must comply with Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (or their replacement). Evaluation criteria and weightings must be published in the ITT. The Government Commercial Function provides guidance on evaluation best practice. Social value must be considered (minimum 10% weighting per PPN 06/20). Standstill periods must be observed before contract award. All evaluation must be documented for audit purposes.

artifacts.name: Contract Variation Request
artifacts.description: A formal request to change the terms of an existing contract — scope, timeline, cost, or deliverables — documenting the reason for change, impact assessment, and proposed new terms.
artifacts.purpose: Contract variations ensure that changes to supplier agreements are managed formally, with proper assessment of impact and appropriate approval. They maintain the integrity of the commercial relationship and protect both parties' interests.
artifacts.whenToUse: Submit when project requirements change in a way that affects the existing contract scope, timeline, or cost. Required before instructing suppliers to do work outside the current contract terms.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Describe the proposed change clearly: what is changing from the current contract terms? Reference specific contract clauses or schedule items being affected.

Explain the rationale: why is this change needed? What has changed since the contract was agreed? Is this driven by new requirements, scope changes, or external factors?

Assess the impact: how does this affect cost, timeline, deliverables, and risk? Get the supplier's assessment of impact as well as your own.

Propose new terms: what should the revised contract say? Include revised costs, timelines, and deliverables.

Obtain appropriate approval: contract variations above certain thresholds require senior commercial or finance approval.
tips: Reference specific contract clauses being varied for legal clarity.
Get the supplier's impact assessment before finalising the variation.
Consider whether the variation is within the scope of the original procurement — significant changes may require re-procurement.
Document the rationale clearly for audit purposes.
Check delegated authority limits — large variations may need senior approval.
commonMistakes: Instructing suppliers to do additional work before the variation is formally agreed.
Not assessing whether the variation is within procurement regulations (material change test).
Not getting appropriate approval before agreeing the variation with the supplier.
Failing to update the contract documentation after the variation is agreed.
Not considering the cumulative effect of multiple small variations.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, contract variations must comply with Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (Regulation 72). Material changes may require re-procurement. The Government Commercial Function provides guidance on variation management. Variations above departmental thresholds require commercial director approval. For contracts on Crown Commercial Service frameworks, framework-specific variation procedures apply. All variations should be recorded in the contract management system.

artifacts.name: Exit Strategy / Transition Plan
artifacts.description: A plan documenting how the organisation will transition away from a supplier or system at the end of a contract, ensuring continuity of service, retention of data and knowledge, and a smooth handover to the replacement.
artifacts.purpose: Exit strategies ensure that the organisation is not locked into a supplier relationship and can transition smoothly when contracts end. They protect against supplier failure, contract disputes, and ensure continuity of service for users.
artifacts.whenToUse: Define at contract inception (not at contract end). Review annually and update as the service evolves. Activate when a contract is approaching its end or when a decision is made to change suppliers.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Identify all assets that need to be transitioned: source code, documentation, data, infrastructure, knowledge, and operational procedures.

Define the transition approach: will the service be brought in-house, moved to a new supplier, or decommissioned? Each requires different planning.

Document data extraction requirements: how will data be exported from the current system? In what format? How will data integrity be verified?

Plan knowledge transfer: what knowledge exists only with the current supplier? How will it be transferred? What documentation is needed?

Define the timeline and milestones: how long will the transition take? What are the key decision points? What is the parallel running period?
tips: Plan the exit at contract start, not contract end — it is much harder to negotiate exit terms later.
Ensure source code escrow or ownership is in the contract from day one.
Include exit provisions in the contract: cooperation obligations, data return, knowledge transfer.
Test data extraction procedures before you need them — do not discover problems during exit.
Plan for a parallel running period where old and new systems operate simultaneously.
commonMistakes: Not planning exit until the contract is ending, leaving insufficient time.
Not including exit provisions in the original contract.
Assuming data can be easily extracted without testing the process.
Underestimating the knowledge transfer effort required.
Not planning for service continuity during the transition period.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, exit strategies are required by the Technology Code of Practice (avoid lock-in). Government contracts should include exit provisions from the outset. The Government Commercial Function provides guidance on exit planning. For critical services, exit strategies should be tested periodically. Open standards and open source reduce exit risk by avoiding proprietary lock-in. CDDO may scrutinise exit provisions as part of spend control reviews.

artifacts.name: Ministerial Submission
artifacts.description: A formal briefing document prepared for a minister, providing information, analysis, and recommendations on a policy or operational matter requiring ministerial awareness or decision.
artifacts.purpose: Ministerial submissions ensure that ministers receive clear, concise, and balanced information to support decision-making. They provide the formal mechanism for seeking ministerial approval or informing ministers of significant developments.
artifacts.whenToUse: Submit when a matter requires ministerial awareness, decision, or approval. Common triggers include significant policy changes, major project decisions, public announcements, and responses to parliamentary questions.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with a clear recommendation or purpose statement — what do you want the minister to do? Approve, note, or decide between options?

Provide concise background — assume the minister has limited context. Explain the issue in plain English without jargon.

Present options with clear pros and cons if seeking a decision. Include the recommended option with rationale.

Address risks and sensitivities: political, media, legal, financial, and operational. Ministers need to know what could go wrong.

Keep it short — ideally one to two pages. Use annexes for detailed supporting information.
tips: Lead with the recommendation — ministers are busy and need to know what you want immediately.
Write in plain English — avoid technical jargon and acronyms.
Be balanced — present risks honestly, do not just tell ministers what they want to hear.
Include handling instructions — is this routine, urgent, or sensitive?
Consider the political context — what questions might the opposition or media ask?
commonMistakes: Burying the recommendation in the middle of the document.
Using technical jargon that ministers and private office staff will not understand.
Not presenting genuine options — a single option dressed as a choice is obvious.
Omitting political and media sensitivities that ministers need to be aware of.
Making submissions too long — ministers have limited time for each decision.
artifacts.governmentContext: Ministerial submissions follow departmental templates and are routed through Private Office. They must comply with the Civil Service Code requirement for honest and impartial advice. For technology decisions, submissions should explain the technical matter in accessible terms and reference alignment with government digital strategy. The Solution Architect may be asked to contribute technical content to submissions about technology investments or service changes.

artifacts.name: Technology Code of Practice Compliance Checklist
artifacts.description: A checklist documenting how a project or service complies with each point of the Government Technology Code of Practice, providing evidence of alignment and noting any areas of non-compliance with justification.
artifacts.purpose: The TCoP checklist demonstrates that technology decisions align with government standards and expectations. It supports spend control submissions, service assessments, and architecture reviews by providing structured compliance evidence.
artifacts.whenToUse: Complete during alpha when making technology decisions. Update during beta as implementation progresses. Reference in spend control submissions and architecture review board papers.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Work through each of the Technology Code of Practice points systematically. For each point, document: whether the project complies, what evidence demonstrates compliance, and any areas of non-compliance with justification.

The TCoP points cover: user needs, accessibility, open source, open standards, cloud first, shared platforms, technology choices, secure by design, privacy, data sharing, integration, and sustainability.

For each point, provide specific evidence rather than generic statements. Reference specific decisions, documents, or practices that demonstrate compliance.

Where full compliance is not possible, explain why and what compensating measures are in place. Non-compliance is sometimes justified but must be explained.

Keep the checklist as a living document — update it as the project progresses and new evidence becomes available.
tips: Be specific with evidence — reference actual documents, decisions, and practices.
Address non-compliance honestly with clear justification rather than claiming false compliance.
Use the checklist proactively to guide decisions, not just retrospectively to document them.
Reference the checklist in spend control submissions to demonstrate alignment.
Review with the team regularly to ensure ongoing compliance as the project evolves.
commonMistakes: Providing generic compliance statements without specific evidence.
Claiming compliance without genuine evidence to support it.
Only completing the checklist for spend control and not using it to guide decisions.
Not updating the checklist as the project progresses.
Treating non-compliance as failure rather than a justified exception with rationale.
artifacts.governmentContext: The Technology Code of Practice is published by CDDO and applies to all government technology projects. Compliance is assessed as part of spend control reviews. The TCoP is not a rigid standard — justified exceptions are acceptable with proper rationale. It aligns with the GDS Service Standard and supports the government digital strategy objectives.

artifacts.name: Accessibility Statement
artifacts.description: A public statement documenting the accessibility of a website or mobile application, including compliance status with WCAG 2.2, known issues, and how users can report accessibility problems or request alternative formats.
artifacts.purpose: Accessibility statements are a legal requirement for public sector websites under the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018. They inform users about accessibility features and limitations, and provide a mechanism for reporting issues.
artifacts.whenToUse: Publish before the service goes into public beta. Update whenever accessibility testing reveals new issues or when issues are resolved. Review at least annually.
artifacts.howToBuild:
State the scope — which website or application does this statement cover?

Declare the compliance status: fully compliant, partially compliant, or not compliant with WCAG 2.2 Level AA. Be honest — claiming full compliance when issues exist is worse than declaring partial compliance.

List known accessibility issues: what problems exist, which WCAG criteria they fail, and when you plan to fix them. Group by severity.

Provide contact information for users to report accessibility problems or request content in alternative formats.

Include the enforcement procedure — how users can escalate if their complaint is not resolved (EHRC in England and Wales, ECNI in Northern Ireland, EHRC in Scotland).
tips: Be honest about known issues — users and regulators respect transparency.
Include a clear mechanism for users to report problems and request alternatives.
Update the statement when issues are fixed or new ones are discovered.
Test with real assistive technology users, not just automated tools.
Follow the GDS sample accessibility statement template for consistency.
commonMistakes: Claiming full compliance without thorough testing.
Not listing known issues, giving users no information about limitations.
Not providing contact details for reporting accessibility problems.
Publishing the statement and never updating it.
Only testing with automated tools and missing issues that require manual testing.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, accessibility statements are legally required under the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) Accessibility Regulations 2018. The GDS provides a sample template that should be followed. Statements must be published in an accessible format on the service itself. The Government Digital Service monitors compliance and the EHRC can take enforcement action. For GDS service assessments, the accessibility statement is reviewed as part of point 5 (make sure everyone can use the service).

artifacts.name: Architecture Vision Document
artifacts.description: A TOGAF Phase A deliverable that provides a high-level aspirational view of the end-state architecture, articulating the business value, key stakeholder concerns, and the scope of the architecture engagement.
artifacts.purpose: The Architecture Vision creates alignment between stakeholders on what the architecture engagement will achieve. It secures buy-in for the architecture work, defines scope and constraints, and provides the basis for detailed architecture development in subsequent TOGAF phases.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create at the start of an architecture engagement (TOGAF Phase A). It precedes detailed architecture development and serves as the mandate for the architecture team to proceed with their work.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the business context: what strategic objectives drive this architecture work? What problems need solving? What opportunities exist?

Define the scope of the architecture engagement: what is included and excluded? Which domains (business, data, application, technology) will be addressed?

Identify key stakeholders and their concerns. Map concerns to architecture views that will address them.

Articulate the target architecture at a high level — enough to communicate the vision without detailed design. Use diagrams to show the conceptual future state.

Define the value proposition: what benefits will the target architecture deliver? How will success be measured?
tips: Keep it visionary but grounded — the vision should be aspirational yet achievable.
Focus on business value, not technical elegance — stakeholders care about outcomes.
Identify and address key stakeholder concerns explicitly.
Use the vision to secure mandate and resources for detailed architecture work.
Keep it concise — this is a vision, not a detailed architecture document.
commonMistakes: Making the vision too detailed — it should inspire direction, not prescribe implementation.
Not linking the architecture vision to business strategy and outcomes.
Ignoring stakeholder concerns that will surface later and derail the work.
Not defining scope clearly, leading to scope creep in the architecture engagement.
Writing the vision without stakeholder input, reducing buy-in.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the Architecture Vision should align with the Government Digital Strategy, departmental transformation plans, and the Technology Code of Practice. It should reference cross-government architecture principles and shared platforms. For major programmes, the vision supports the strategic case in the business case and informs IPA gateway reviews.

artifacts.name: Architecture Roadmap (TOGAF)
artifacts.description: A TOGAF deliverable showing the timeline for transitioning from the baseline architecture to the target architecture, including work packages, milestones, and the sequence of transition architectures.
artifacts.purpose: The TOGAF Architecture Roadmap provides a time-sequenced view of how the architecture will evolve, enabling programme planning, resource allocation, and investment decisions. It shows the path from current state to target state in manageable increments.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during TOGAF Phase E (Opportunities and Solutions) and Phase F (Migration Planning). Update as implementation progresses and priorities shift.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with the gap analysis between baseline and target architecture. Identify all the changes needed across business, data, application, and technology domains.

Group changes into work packages that can be delivered together. Consider dependencies, risk, and value delivery when grouping.

Sequence work packages on a timeline considering: dependencies between packages, resource availability, risk (do high-risk items early), and value delivery (deliver value incrementally).

Define transition architectures — stable intermediate states between baseline and target. Each transition should be operational and deliver value.

Include decision points where the roadmap may need to adapt based on outcomes from earlier phases.
tips: Align with financial planning cycles — work packages should map to budget periods.
Show dependencies clearly — they drive the sequence more than anything else.
Include both build and decommission activities.
Mark decision points where the roadmap may pivot.
Keep it at the right level of detail — too detailed and it becomes unmanageable.
commonMistakes: Creating a roadmap that is too detailed and becomes stale quickly.
Not showing dependencies between work packages.
Ignoring decommissioning of legacy systems.
Not including decision points where the roadmap may need to adapt.
Treating the roadmap as fixed rather than a living plan.

artifacts.name: Architecture Requirements Specification
artifacts.description: A TOGAF deliverable that provides a quantitative set of architecture requirements, including functional, non-functional, and constraint requirements that the architecture must satisfy.
artifacts.purpose: The Architecture Requirements Specification provides a formal, measurable set of requirements that the architecture must meet, bridging the gap between business requirements and architecture design. It ensures the architecture is designed to meet specific, verifiable criteria.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during TOGAF Phase B-D (Business, Information Systems, and Technology Architecture) as requirements are identified. Reference during Phase E when evaluating solution options.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Gather requirements from multiple sources: business requirements, stakeholder concerns, existing architecture principles, regulatory obligations, and technology constraints.

Categorise requirements by domain: business architecture requirements, data architecture requirements, application architecture requirements, and technology architecture requirements.

Make each requirement specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART). Avoid vague requirements that cannot be verified.

Prioritise requirements and identify conflicts between them. Document trade-off decisions where requirements compete.

Trace requirements to their source (stakeholder, regulation, principle) for accountability and change management.
tips: Make every requirement measurable — if you cannot test it, it is not a requirement.
Trace requirements to their source for accountability.
Identify conflicts between requirements early and document trade-off decisions.
Prioritise using MoSCoW to guide architecture decisions.
Review with stakeholders to confirm requirements are correctly captured.
commonMistakes: Writing vague requirements that cannot be verified.
Not prioritising, implying all requirements are equally important.
Not tracing requirements to their source.
Ignoring conflicts between competing requirements.
Not reviewing with stakeholders for validation.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, architecture requirements should reference the Technology Code of Practice, GDS Service Standard, and relevant legislation. Accessibility requirements (WCAG 2.2 AA) are legally mandated. Security requirements should align with NCSC guidance. Requirements should be proportionate to the risk and value of the service.

artifacts.name: Architecture Definition Document
artifacts.description: A TOGAF deliverable that provides a comprehensive view of the architecture across all domains (business, data, application, technology), showing the baseline, target, and gap analysis for each domain.
artifacts.purpose: The Architecture Definition Document is the primary output of TOGAF Phase B-D, providing a complete and coherent architecture description that can be used to guide implementation. It brings together all architecture views into a single reference.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during TOGAF Phases B, C, and D as each architecture domain is developed. It is the main deliverable of the architecture development cycle and feeds into implementation planning.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Structure the document around the four TOGAF domains: Business Architecture, Data Architecture, Application Architecture, and Technology Architecture.

For each domain, document: the baseline (current state), the target (future state), and the gap analysis (what needs to change).

Use ArchiMate or UML diagrams to visualise each architecture domain. Show relationships between domains — how business processes map to applications, how applications use data, and how technology supports applications.

Include architecture decisions made during development, with rationale. Reference ADRs for detailed decision records.

Validate the architecture against the requirements specification to ensure all requirements are addressed.
tips: Use consistent notation across all domains for readability.
Show cross-domain relationships — architecture domains are not independent.
Include both diagrams and narrative — diagrams alone are insufficient.
Validate against requirements to ensure completeness.
Keep it maintainable — structure for easy updates as the architecture evolves.
commonMistakes: Treating domains in isolation without showing cross-domain relationships.
Not including gap analysis, making it unclear what needs to change.
Making it too detailed for its purpose — it should guide, not prescribe.
Not validating against requirements, potentially missing gaps.
Creating a document so large that nobody reads or maintains it.

Map concerns to specific architecture views for traceability.
Include both technical and non-technical stakeholders.

artifacts.name: GDS Service Assessment Preparation Pack
artifacts.description: A comprehensive preparation pack for teams approaching a GDS service assessment, including self-assessment against the 14 points of the Service Standard, evidence inventory, demo plan, and team briefing materials.
artifacts.purpose: The preparation pack ensures the team is fully prepared for a GDS service assessment, maximising the chance of a positive outcome. It identifies gaps in evidence, prepares team members for questions, and ensures the demo showcases the service effectively.
artifacts.whenToUse: Begin preparation 4-6 weeks before the scheduled assessment. Use for alpha, beta, and live assessments. The pack evolves as evidence is gathered and gaps are addressed.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start with a self-assessment against all 14 points of the Service Standard at the appropriate phase level (expectations differ between alpha, beta, and live).

For each point, inventory the evidence available: research findings, design artefacts, technical documentation, metrics, and team practices.

Identify gaps — where is evidence weak or missing? Create an action plan to address gaps before the assessment.

Prepare the demo: what user journeys will you show? What technical capabilities will you demonstrate? Ensure the demo environment is stable.

Brief the team: who will answer questions on which topics? What are the likely challenging questions? Practice with a mock assessment.
tips: Start preparation early — 4-6 weeks minimum before the assessment.
Conduct a mock assessment with colleagues from other teams.
Be honest about gaps — assessors respect transparency and want to help.
Prepare the whole team, not just the product owner — assessors ask different people.
The assessment is a conversation, not a presentation — prepare for dialogue, not slides.
commonMistakes: Starting preparation too late and rushing to fill evidence gaps.
Only preparing the product owner and leaving other team members unprepared.
Treating it as a pass/fail exam rather than a peer review conversation.
Over-preparing presentations when assessors want natural conversation.
Hiding problems rather than being transparent about challenges and plans.

artifacts.name: Policy-Technology Alignment Document
artifacts.description: A document demonstrating how technology decisions and architecture align with and enable policy objectives, bridging the gap between policy intent and digital delivery.
artifacts.purpose: Policy-technology alignment ensures that digital services faithfully implement policy intent while leveraging technology to improve outcomes. It prevents the common problem of technology teams building something that does not match what policy teams intended.
artifacts.whenToUse: Create during discovery when translating policy requirements into service design. Update during alpha and beta as the implementation reveals policy interpretation challenges.
artifacts.howToBuild:
Start by documenting the policy intent: what outcomes does the policy aim to achieve? What are the eligibility criteria, rules, and exceptions?

Map policy rules to system behaviour: how will each policy rule be implemented in the digital service? Where are there ambiguities that need policy clarification?

Identify where technology enables better policy outcomes: automation of decisions, real-time eligibility checking, proactive notifications, data-driven insights.

Document policy interpretation decisions: where the policy is ambiguous, how has the team interpreted it for implementation? Get policy team sign-off on interpretations.

Plan for policy changes: how will the system accommodate future policy changes? What is configurable vs hard-coded?
tips: Involve policy teams throughout, not just at the start — interpretation questions arise during implementation.
Document policy interpretation decisions explicitly and get sign-off.
Design for policy change — rules and thresholds should be configurable.
Use examples and scenarios to validate that the system implements policy correctly.
Bridge the language gap — translate between policy language and technical language.
commonMistakes: Building the service without ongoing policy team involvement.
Not documenting policy interpretation decisions, leading to disputes later.
Hard-coding policy rules that are likely to change.
Assuming policy intent is clear when it is often ambiguous in edge cases.
Not testing the implementation against policy scenarios with policy team input.
artifacts.governmentContext: In UK government, the gap between policy intent and digital delivery is a common source of problems. Policy teams and digital teams often speak different languages. The GDS Service Standard expects teams to understand the policy context (point 2: solve a whole problem). For services implementing legislation, legal interpretation may be needed. Policy changes (e.g., budget announcements, new regulations) must be accommodated quickly.
